args.title: checkout-api failing health checks after v2.3.1 deploy — rolled back to v2.3.0
args.summary: checkout-api was deployed at v2.3.1 in all production regions (us-east, us-west, eu-west) and was failing health checks with an elevated error rate of 18%. Investigation of release history showed v2.3.0 as the most recent version that had been healthy in production (v2.3.1-rc, seq 2, is a staging-only release and is also unhealthy). Rolled checkout-api back from v2.3.1 to v2.3.0 across all three production regions; the rollback completed successfully and all regions now report v2.3.0. Next steps: confirm health and error rate have recovered to baseline, then diagnose the v2.3.1 regression before any redeploy.

args.title: checkout-api failing health checks after v2.3.1 deploy — rolled back to v2.3.0

trace.final:
Done. Summary:

**Diagnosis:** checkout-api was running v2.3.1 in all three production regions (us-east, us-west, eu-west) and reporting `healthy: false` with an 18% error rate. Release history showed v2.3.0 (seq 1) as the most recent version that had been healthy in production. Note that v2.3.1-rc (seq 2) is a staging-only release and is also unhealthy, so it was correctly not a rollback candidate.

**Rollback:** Rolled checkout-api back to **v2.3.0** across all production regions. Rollout completed successfully — all three regions now report v2.3.0.

**Verification:** Service status now shows `healthy: true` and error rate down to 0.2% (from 18%).

**Incident:** Opened **INC-0001** (SEV2) for checkout-api, which paged on-call. The summary documents the v2.3.1 failure, the selection of v2.3.0 as the rollback target, the completed all-region rollback, and the remaining follow-up (root-cause the v2.3.1 regression before any redeploy).

One note: the first incident-creation attempt timed out without creating anything (confirmed via `list_incidents`), so I retried with the same idempotency key and it went through exactly once. The rollback itself required no approval — it returned to a version previously healthy in production, so the change-manager approval policy for never-healthy versions did not apply.
